ECE 6390 / Waves and fields

Polarization

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how the electric-field trajectory affects coupling to a receiving antenna.

At a fixed location, two orthogonal transverse components combine into a line, ellipse, or circle. Their relative amplitudes and phase difference determine the locus of the electric-field tip.

For normalized complex polarization vectors, coupling is |eᵣ†eₜ|². Two linear polarizations separated by angle ψ have a power coupling factor cos²ψ.

Equal orthogonal components in quadrature form circular polarization. An ideal linear receiving antenna extracts half of that wave's available power at every linear orientation, assuming the remaining antenna and link factors are matched.

Example

A 45° mismatch between linear polarizations gives cos²45° = 1/2, corresponding to a 3.01 dB polarization loss.

    Practice

    1. Why does rotating an ideal linear receive antenna fail to recover all of an incident circularly polarized wave's power?

    Resolve equal quadrature components onto any one fixed linear axis.

    Every fixed linear axis receives one half of the circular wave's average power. Rotation changes the selected component's phase, while its average power fraction remains 1/2.
